strengths: The paper addresses a concrete and practically important limitation of LLM-based RTL generation: optimizing functional correctness together with hardware PPA metrics, rather than treating PPA as a post-processing concern.

The proposed framework is technically coherent: hierarchical EDA-derived rewards, fail-fast gating, advantage-level reward aggregation, curriculum weighting, and preference-conditioned PPA objectives are well motivated for this multi-objective setting.

The empirical evaluation is broad relative to the RTL-generation literature, covering VerilogEval, RTLLM v1.1/v2.0, multiple 7B base models, comparisons to specialized baselines and GPT-series models, plus ablations over reward components, training stages, and RL variants.

The reported gains are substantial, especially on RTLLM functional pass rates and normalized EDAP, and the paper includes useful analyses of runtime, optimization strategy categories, robustness across PDK/synthesis configurations, and a larger-design AutoSilicon setting.

The implementation details in the appendix are more complete than average, including training hyperparameters, compute budget, reward evaluation pipeline, pass@k and PPA metric definitions, and prompt templates.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is only partial. The data-generation pipeline depends on proprietary or unavailable models such as GPT-5 and DeepSeek-R1, and the paper promises open sourcing but does not provide an artifact link in the manuscript. Reproducing the exact training data and testbenches may therefore be difficult.

The evaluation may be vulnerable to benchmark contamination or near-duplicate leakage because training data are curated from online repositories and then filtered against benchmark cases, but the paper does not describe the deduplication procedure rigorously enough for Verilog designs where structurally similar solutions are common.

Functional correctness depends heavily on generated testbenches. The paper says GPT-5-generated testbenches are validated, but it does not convincingly establish that they are complete or equivalent to formal/spec-level verification, so some pass@k and PPA comparisons could reward designs that satisfy weak tests rather than full intended behavior.

The PPA evaluation protocol has possible selection bias: PPA metrics are averaged only over functionally correct generated designs/tasks, and the treatment of failures, N/A cases, and differing success sets across models is not fully convincing. This can make EDAP comparisons optimistic for models with lower pass rates or different failure patterns.

Several claims are stronger than the evidence supports, such as learning robust micro-architectural optimization principles and scaling to production-level RTL. The largest-design experiment is useful but still limited, and the case study is anecdotal.

The novelty is incremental in parts: EDA-in-the-loop reward optimization, GRPO/DAPO-style RL, reward gating, and preference weighting are sensible combinations, but the paper should more sharply distinguish what is algorithmically new from an effective engineering integration.

The work is relevant to code generation and NLP for programming, but it is closer to EDA than mainstream computational linguistics. For ACL main-conference consideration, the paper would benefit from clearer framing of the language/modeling contribution beyond RTL-specific engineering.

strengths: The paper addresses a concrete and practically important problem: RTL generation that jointly considers functional correctness and hardware PPA metrics, rather than treating Verilog generation as only a code-syntax task.

The proposed closed-loop training setup is conceptually reasonable: compiler, simulator, synthesis, and PPA feedback are natural reward sources for this domain, and the hierarchical gating mechanism is a sensible way to reduce expensive EDA evaluations.

The empirical section is broad, covering VerilogEval, RTLLM v1.1/v2.0, design-priority prompting, reward ablations, RL-method ablations, runtime analysis, sensitivity to PDK/synthesis settings, and a scalability experiment.

The reported gains, if reproducible, are substantial across both functional correctness and EDAP-style hardware metrics, and the ablations generally support the importance of PPA rewards, curriculum weighting, and advantage-level aggregation.
weaknesses: The work is only marginally positioned for ACL/NLP. The core contribution is primarily an EDA/toolchain-integrated RL system for hardware design, with limited discussion of what is learned about language, code generation methodology beyond this specialized setting, or broader NLP relevance.

Reproducibility is a serious concern. The abstract contains an unfinished open-source statement, while the appendix only says the authors will release code and scripts. The training data sources, filtering procedure, benchmark decontamination, exact prompts, tool versions, synthesis constraints, and generated testbenches are not specified sufficiently for independent reproduction.

The evaluation relies heavily on generated testbenches, reportedly produced by GPT-5, but the paper gives little evidence that these testbenches are complete, unbiased, or comparable across models. Passing weak or automatically generated tests is not the same as functional correctness, especially for hardware modules.

The metric aggregation may overstate PPA quality. PPA is computed after filtering to functionally correct designs, and the final performance averages over successfully generated tasks, which can bias comparisons in favor of models with different failure patterns. N/A/failure cases are not clearly penalized in the EDAP summaries.

There are possible data leakage and benchmark contamination concerns. The authors say benchmark cases are filtered out, but the training data are scraped from online repositories and augmented using powerful commercial models; the paper does not provide enough detail to verify that benchmark-equivalent designs, solutions, or testbenches were excluded.

Several claims are stronger than the evidence supports. Statements such as learning robust micro-architectural coding patterns or production-level scalability are based on limited benchmark settings and small/unclear task sets, while the case study is anecdotal and uses a textbook optimization that synthesis tools may already infer.

The methodological novelty relative to existing GRPO/DAPO-style RL with multi-component rewards is not fully established. CDPO appears to combine known ingredients: reward normalization, curriculum weights, preference-conditioned weighting, and PPO-style clipping. The paper needs a clearer technical distinction and stronger controlled comparisons.

The paper contains presentation and clarity problems that undermine confidence: malformed text and tables, missing spaces, incomplete artifact sentence, inconsistent naming, vague descriptions of commercial model use, and insufficiently documented hyperparameters/toolchain details in the main text.

Some reported results are surprising and need more scrutiny, such as very large jumps from RL on standard VerilogEval and strong PPA gains across PDKs/tools. The paper does not provide confidence intervals, statistical tests, per-task breakdowns for most claims, or enough information about number of tasks and sampling variance.

Overall, the work may become publishable after substantial revision, but in its current form the claims are not adequately supported or reproducible enough for a positive Findings recommendation, and the fit for ACL main conference is weak.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: moving RTL code generation beyond functional correctness toward synthesizable and PPA-aware designs. This is a meaningful contribution for code-generation research with a clear connection to LLM alignment using external tool feedback.

The proposed framework is technically coherent. The hierarchical reward design, EDA-tool gating, advantage-level aggregation, curriculum weighting, and preference-conditioned PPA objectives are well motivated for the multi-objective and expensive-feedback setting.

Empirical results are strong across several benchmarks and base models. The paper reports gains on VerilogEval, RTLLM v1.1/v2.0, PPA metrics, and larger AutoSilicon-style designs, with consistent improvements over strong Verilog-specific and general LLM baselines.

The ablations are useful and support the main methodological claims: removing function/PPA rewards, curriculum weighting, advantage aggregation, or preference vectors degrades correctness, synthesizability, or PPA outcomes.

The paper includes helpful implementation and evaluation details, including toolchain components, reward computation, training resources, hyperparameters, runtime acceleration, and prompt templates. This substantially improves clarity compared with many tool-integrated RL papers.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is still not fully established. The abstract says the artifact is open-source but the statement appears incomplete, and no repository or concrete artifact link is provided. Some key data sources, filtering rules, generated testbenches, and benchmark decontamination procedures are only described at a high level.

The evaluation depends heavily on LLM-generated testbenches and EDA-tool measurements, but the paper does not sufficiently validate the testbench quality or quantify false positives/false negatives in functional correctness. This is important because weak or biased testbenches could inflate pass rates.

Several performance metrics are averaged only over functionally correct generated designs or successfully generated tasks, which may introduce selection effects when comparing models with different success rates. The paper reports pass rates separately, but the PPA aggregation protocol could still favor models that produce fewer valid candidates unless handled very carefully.

The comparison protocol is not always fully aligned across settings. For example, some results choose the best metric across multiple attempts, while other tables report max/avg/min over candidates. The paper should more clearly justify these choices and include statistical uncertainty or repeated-run variance.

The novelty is solid but not transformative: the main technical ideas combine known RL-for-verifiable-rewards machinery, curriculum weighting, reward normalization, and tool feedback in a well-engineered RTL setting. The contribution is valuable, but the core algorithmic advance over GRPO/DAPO-style methods is incremental.

The work is highly relevant to code generation and tool-augmented LLMs, but its center of gravity is also strongly in EDA/CAD. For an ACL main-conference paper, the authors should more explicitly articulate the NLP/code-generation lessons that generalize beyond Verilog and hardware design.
